mcqs.question: Why do long parameter lists correlate with bugs in the same way long methods do?
options: They both overload the reader's short-term memory instead of letting the type system carry meaning
They both make the compiler generate slower machine code
They both are illegal in most modern languages and require a linter override
They both only matter for languages without static typing
mcqs.explanation: A long method's branches and a long parameter list's unlabeled args both force the reader to hold meaning in working memory instead of getting it from names or types. There's no compiler-speed effect, no language forbids them outright, and the problem exists in statically typed languages too — `true, false, null, 3` is just as opaque in Java as in Python.

mcqs.question: How does a Large Class (God Class) smell differ from the God Object anti-pattern?
options: They're the same thing described at two different scopes: a local class-level smell versus its architecture-level, whole-codebase consequence
A Large Class only happens in interpreted languages, while a God Object only happens in compiled ones
A Large Class is always caused by inheritance, while a God Object is always caused by composition
There is no relationship between the two terms
mcqs.explanation: Large Class is the local smell you catch reading one file; God Object is what happens architecturally once that overloaded class becomes a dependency half the system routes through. They're related by scope, not by language feature or by inheritance-versus-composition — that distinction isn't what separates them.

mcqs.question: What's the diagnostic question for spotting a data clump worth extracting into its own type?
options: Do these values always appear together as parameters, and would passing only some of them ever make sense?
Are there more than two parameters in the method signature, regardless of what they represent?
Is at least one of the parameters a string type?
Has the method been modified more than three times in version control?
mcqs.explanation: The data-clump test is about co-occurrence and meaning, not raw parameter count, data type, or edit history — three primitives that happen to sit next to each other but are used independently aren't a clump. Street/city/zip qualify because they always travel together and rarely make sense apart.

mcqs.question: In the Address value-object refactor, what concretely improves once street/city/zip become one `Address` type instead of three loose parameters?
options: Zip validation happens once at construction, so it's impossible to end up with an invalid Address passed around the system
The code runs measurably faster because fewer arguments are passed on the stack
The method signatures become longer, which makes call sites more explicit
It removes the need for any tests on the shipping or billing methods
mcqs.explanation: The real win is centralizing validation: before, every caller could independently forget to validate the zip; after, the constructor guarantees it. Method signatures actually get shorter, not longer; there's no meaningful stack-passing speed difference at this scale; and the refactor doesn't remove the need for tests — it makes the tests you do write more meaningful.

mcqs.question: You spot a smelly 200-line method you need to touch for an unrelated feature, and it has zero test coverage. What's the correct move before refactoring it?
options: Refactor it immediately in the same commit as your feature change, since you're already in the file
Leave it exactly as-is forever and never refactor any method without pre-existing tests
Write a characterization test first to pin down current behavior, then refactor in a separate commit from the feature change
Ask a teammate to manually re-test the whole module after you refactor, instead of writing any automated test
mcqs.explanation: Refactoring without a safety net risks silently changing behavior; a characterization test captures what the code currently does so you can refactor with confidence, and keeping it in its own commit isolates any regression. Refactoring blind in the same commit as a feature change is the risky path this pitfall warns against, and 'never refactor without pre-existing tests' overcorrects — you can add the test yourself first.
